title: The cowherd boy's stone
hook: a cowherd's boy watches a king worship Shiva, then sets up a plain stone of his own
carry: shiva is seen by everyone, not only priests
tomorrow: a thief breaks into a temple on Shivaratri night. what does Shiva do?

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Rudram bows to anger, then asks for peace, a hymn the gods offered to calm the archer. Today, the same opening section looks up at the sky.
screen: `A BOW TO ANGER.` · `TODAY: WHO HAS SEEN HIM?`

segments.voice: In Ujjain, the Shiva Purana says, King Chandrasena worships Shiva as Mahakala, the great lord of time, with all the splendor a king can offer. A cowherd's little boy watches. He goes home, finds a plain stone, sets it up, and worships it the way he saw the king do, with leaves and whatever he has. His mother, tired of it, throws the stone away. The boy cries until he falls asleep. When he wakes, a shining shrine stands where his stone had been.
screen: `A KING WORSHIPS MAHAKALA.` → `A COWHERD'S BOY, A PLAIN STONE.` → `A SHINING SHRINE.`

segments.voice: Ujjain's Mahakala is still one of the twelve jyotirlingas, the great shrines of Shiva as light, and this story belongs to it: a child with no priest and no Sanskrit. The Rudram said it first. Still in its opening section, it points to a figure crossing the sky, copper, red, brown, wholly auspicious, the blue-throated one, glowing. Then the surprising line. The cowherds have seen him. The women carrying water have seen him. All beings have seen him. May he, seen, be kind to us. Some readers, following the old commentary of Sayana, take that figure as the sun. On that reading, Rudra isn't locked away in a temple or a cave. He's in plain view every morning, and the first people the hymn names as having seen him aren't sages or kings. They're a cowherd and a woman fetching water, in the middle of their work. Here's the Hindu teaching under both: Shiva is seen by everyone, not only priests. Temples have priests and rules, and Hindus value them. But the one worshipped there isn't hidden from anyone who looks. It's why so many Hindus keep a small shrine at home, why a stone under a tree can be a place of worship, and why the morning offering of water to the rising sun needs no one's permission. So when someone asks if they're allowed to come, if they're Hindu enough, if they know enough Sanskrit, the hymn has already answered. The cowherds have seen him.
screen: `MAHAKALA, A JYOTIRLINGA.` · `THE COWHERDS HAVE SEEN HIM.` · `SEEN, MAY HE BE KIND.` · `A SHRINE AT HOME, A STONE BY A TREE.` · then, large: `SEEN BY EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Do what many Hindus do at sunrise, with whatever light you have. Face a window or a lamp, hold a cup of water, and pour a little out slowly, into a plant or a bowl, as an offering to the light. Remember the cowherd's boy with his stone, and the women carrying water. If you pray, say Om namah shivaya, or greet the light as the hymn does. If you don't, just look, and let looking be enough.
The Rudram. Today's passage: the copper-red one crossing the sky, seen by the cowherds, the women carrying water, and all beings.
Your line: Shiva is seen by everyone, not only priests. The cowherds have seen him. I'll be here tomorrow.
